items.title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, a 816B-parameter multimodal AI model optimized for Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with 1M-token context window and agentic capabilities [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Meta has launched Muse Spark Open, an 816 billion parameter multimodal AI model designed for complex coding, multi-step reasoning, and long-horizon tasks. The model supports a 1 million token context window and is optimized to run on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios using the MLX framework, enabling powerful on-device AI workflows. Muse Spark Open is available through multiple API platforms and cloud providers, with weights downloadable from Amazon SageMaker, Google Cloud, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models. It supports various inference engines and hardware optimizations, allowing developers to customize it via PyTorch. Meta has implemented safety measures and released the model under a license permitting many free commercial uses.

items.title: Researcher finds neural networks are inherently interpretable, challenging prior beliefs about polysemanticity and superposition in image and language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A researcher studying neural networks in image and language models has concluded that these networks are inherently interpretable, contradicting earlier views that networks pack concepts arbitrarily through polysemanticity and superposition. The study suggests that what appeared as complex entanglement was actually a form of recursive generalization, making mechanistic interpretability more feasible than previously thought. Improvements in network architecture have increased neuron interpretability, with modern models showing clearer, more legible structures across scales. This challenges the prior assumption that neural networks require complex unfolding or reconstruction to be understood.

items.title: Krea 3 launches a production-ready image editing model that edits only specified areas, operates at native 2K resolution, and completes edits faster and cheaper than competitors [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Krea 3 is a new image editing model designed for production use, enabling precise edits that change only user-specified parts of an image while preserving the rest. It completes edits in about 8 seconds at a cost of approximately $0.06 per image, outperforming similar models in speed and cost efficiency. The model supports up to eight reference images, matches exact colors by hex code, and maintains character consistency across edits, all rendered natively at 2K resolution. The model is integrated into workflows for designers working on posters, branding, and covers, allowing rapid, voice-driven edits and offering 251 launch presets. Krea 3 is distributed through leading organizations and aims to streamline image editing by reducing wait times and costs while maintaining high precision and detail. The company provides support for prototyping, development, and scaling AI solutions with Krea 3.

items.title: Developer uses AI to reverse engineer hardware drivers, creating a generic harness to aid Linux support for unsupported devices [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: A developer applied AI tools, specifically Claude, to reverse engineer hardware drivers for devices lacking Linux support, such as a Plustek 8200i scanner and a laptop MIPI camera. By capturing USB traffic and comparing Windows driver behavior with Linux attempts, the AI helped generate working drivers and patches, significantly reducing the manual effort typically required. The developer created a generic harness called hw-harness to automate capturing and diffing USB traffic between Windows and Linux drivers, enabling AI to identify driver bugs and propose fixes. This approach avoids copying code and instead extracts configuration data from Windows drivers, making it easier for others to apply AI-assisted reverse engineering to their own hardware challenges.

items.title: Researchers propose confidence-calibrated controller for evaluator-guided test-time reasoning that reduces compute by up to 30% while maintaining utility [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce a compute-aware three-action controller for evaluator-guided reasoning that decides whether to trust the current answer, fallback, or spend more inference based on predicted success and compute cost. The approach includes a local action-gap analysis and expected regret bounds to guide learning and calibration of confidence estimates with uncertainty penalties for ambiguous decisions. Evaluations on width expansion and revision tasks show the controller improves utility over fixed policies while reducing normalized online compute by about 30% and 16%, respectively, framing evaluator-guided reasoning as resource allocation under uncertainty rather than uniformly stronger reasoning.

items.title: Researchers present LEV, a looped decision model that improves accuracy by rerunning layers for deeper reasoning without generating tokens, achieving up to 76.2% accuracy on JevBench [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce LEV, a decision model that enhances reasoning depth by looping through its layers multiple times instead of generating text tokens. LEV is built on a language model pretrained as a loop and can adjust its reasoning depth per question, improving accuracy especially on harder problems. Experiments show that a 2.6 billion parameter LEV model increases accuracy from 63.2% at one loop to 76.2% at four loops on the JevBench dataset, while saving computation with an on-demand stopping mechanism. The model's design allows a single checkpoint to operate at various depths, trained jointly across all steps. On locked test sets, LEV models with 1.4 billion and 3 billion parameters outperform comparable non-looped models by 5.4 to 8.8 accuracy points while maintaining latency under 50 milliseconds. This approach offers a flexible trade-off between computational cost and accuracy, particularly benefiting difficult decision tasks.

items.title: Athanor system enables autonomous AI agents to post-train a base model into a generalist model matching official instruct versions in 104 hours [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Athanor is an open agent-native system designed for autonomous post-training research on GPUs, allowing AI agents full autonomy to improve base models without external guidance. In a 104-hour experiment, four Claude Opus 5.5 agents collaboratively enhanced the Qwen3-4B-Base model, achieving performance comparable to or exceeding the official instruct version on multiple evaluation suites. The agents independently managed data processing, algorithm modification, hyperparameter tuning, and result analysis within a sandboxed environment, using known methods such as supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, weight merging, and self-distillation. This demonstration marks the first time frontier agents have autonomously post-trained a raw base model into a cross-domain generalist model, suggesting that current AI agents possess the engineering and research capabilities to conduct complex autonomous AI research.

items.title: Researchers introduce Kolab dataset to benchmark human-AI collaboration in long-horizon professional workflows with 115+ hours of recordings from 50 professionals [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers have developed Kolab, a dataset containing over 115 hours of screen recordings of 50 professionals from 40 occupations collaborating with AI agents on complex, long-horizon tasks. The dataset includes participants' judgments on collaboration and output quality, aiming to better understand how humans interact with AI agents beyond simple automation benchmarks. Kolab highlights the need for AI agents to anticipate whether experts will adopt, modify, or reject their contributions and to assess collaboration quality without constant feedback. Analysis shows that current AI models tend to overestimate collaboration effectiveness and struggle to differentiate between high- and low-quality interactions, indicating that frontier agents are not yet capable of fully understanding long-term human-agent collaboration in professional settings.

items.title: Researchers identify fundamental limits in automated self-improvement evaluation for autonomous AI agents, showing no terminating procedure can guarantee both reliability and non-conservatism in general settings [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers analyze the challenge of safely enabling autonomous AI agents to self-improve by proposing updates to their own components. They formalize the problem by modeling agents as programs and defining improvement via a semantic score that may be uncomputable, demonstrating that no terminating, computable gate can reliably approve only genuine improvements without missing some, due to inherent self-referential limitations. The study distinguishes between general unbounded settings, where correctness guarantees fail, and bounded practical regimes with finite evaluation and proposal budgets, where exhaustive simulation can yield reliable search procedures. However, even in bounded settings, sequences of accepted updates can misleadingly increase bounded scores while the true semantic quality declines, highlighting intrinsic challenges in designing safe self-improving AI systems.

items.title: DeciCAD introduces a domain-native harness for CAD agents that improves action policy learning and execution through supervised fine-tuning and geometry-grounded reinforcement learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: DeciCAD presents a new approach for computer-aided design (CAD) agents by using a domain-specific harness that defines semantic actions, observations, and state transitions. This harness shapes the decision space for large language model agents, enabling improved policy learning and execution in the CAD domain characterized by persistent state and geometric constraints. The system uses a learning pipeline combining supervised fine-tuning and online reinforcement learning to enhance agent performance. Evaluated across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves higher F1 scores and intersection over union (IoU) metrics while significantly reducing model output tokens compared to a general-purpose coding harness. Its supervised fine-tuning policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms coding-based policies, with reinforcement learning further increasing geometry availability and F1 to 0.7880. These results highlight the impact of the harness-defined decision space on agent behavior and policy learning in CAD tasks.

items.title: Researchers develop MLExpert, a 35B parameter agentic model for autonomous machine learning engineering that improves optimization performance on MLE-Bench Lite and generalizes to other tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: Researchers propose MLExpert, a 35 billion parameter Mixture-of-Experts agentic model designed for autonomous long-horizon machine learning engineering (MLE) optimization. The model uses a post-training method involving hierarchical supervised fine-tuning and Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning to improve experiment orchestration and optimization strategies based on execution feedback. MLExpert was evaluated on MLE-Bench Lite, where it increased the average medal rate from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger models like Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. The team developed the Kaggle-MLE Factory to create executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. MLExpert's learned optimization capabilities also improved results on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, indicating its potential to generalize across various machine learning engineering tasks.

items.title: Researchers explore three diffusion-LLM parameterizations for permutation generation, evaluating their performance on Amazon recommendation reranking tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied permutation generation with language models using three diffusion-LLM parameterizations: hard-assignment prediction over shuffled candidate-index sequences, soft-assignment prediction over doubly stochastic matrices, and direct ordering-score prediction followed by sorting. They evaluated these methods on recommendation reranking across three Amazon domains with candidate sets of size 10 and 20, finding that hard- and soft-assignment variants achieved Recall@1 comparable to a constrained masked-diffusion baseline, while direct ordering-score prediction guaranteed valid permutations without additional normalization steps. The study showed that additional function evaluations did not consistently improve ranking quality and that the effectiveness depended strongly on the state representation and training objective. The results suggest that corruption, prediction parameterization, objective, and decoder should be designed jointly for permutation diffusion with language-model denoisers to optimize performance.

items.title: Researchers present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that processes a case once to answer multiple typed questions with higher accuracy and lower latency than separate cross-encoders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce Verdict-MQ, a 395M-parameter open encoder designed to automate organizational decision-making by reading a case once and answering multiple typed questions independently. The model uses a structured attention mask to ensure question independence and option order invariance, outperforming a 421M-parameter specialist model on a typed-decisions benchmark with higher accuracy and better agreement with benchmark labels. Verdict-MQ shows mixed results on other benchmarks like RACE, BoolQ, and MultiRC, winning on MultiRC but losing on RACE and BoolQ due to training instability. A controlled comparison reveals that providing each question with its own question-aware state copy improves accuracy on some benchmarks but increases latency by 1.4 to 2.5 times, while Verdict-MQ maintains invariance guarantees without measurable latency cost on typed decisions.

items.title: Researchers propose CoTranslator to convert reverse chain-of-thought responses into verified forward responses for efficient reasoning distillation in AI models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: CoTranslator is a new method designed to improve reasoning distillation by translating reverse chain-of-thought (CoT) responses, which condition on known answers, into verified forward CoT responses that do not rely on answers. This approach addresses the inefficiency and potential mismatch in existing methods by training on a small set of paired reverse and forward responses to enable large-scale generation and verification of training data for student AI models. Evaluated across six student models on six mathematics benchmarks, CoTranslator improved average accuracy by up to 5.82 percentage points over semantic suppression methods. It retained 95.0% of the accuracy of rejection sampling while using only 35.9% of the compute for two 4-billion-parameter students. The method also transferred effectively without retraining to new datasets, different teachers, and STEM problems, boosting average STEM accuracy by 4.88 and 4.31 percentage points for 4B and 8B parameter students, respectively. These results demonstrate that CoTranslator offers an efficient and transferable solution for reasoning distillation, reducing computational costs while maintaining high accuracy across diverse tasks and models.

items.title: Researchers find majority-vote rewards in reinforcement learning track verifiable rewards due to error incoherence across prompts, preserving update direction despite label errors [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: A new study explains why reinforcement learning using self-generated labels, such as majority votes over a model's own outputs, often achieves similar gains to training with verifiable rewards. The researchers show that at practical batch sizes, individual prompt gradients contribute minimally to output changes, so incorrect labels only affect learning if errors align coherently across prompts. They demonstrate that majority-vote updates closely match gold-standard updates when errors are incoherent, and that random label flips up to 30% do not disrupt the update direction. The team measured per-response gradients across five models and found majority-vote errors as incoherent as random noise, with update directions agreeing as closely as independent gold updates. However, label errors following a shared pattern or reward models favoring certain responses degrade this alignment. While the equivalence between majority-vote and gold-reward updates holds locally at checkpoints, gold-reward training still outperforms on held-out accuracy. The findings highlight that error coherence, rather than error rate, determines when self-generated labels can substitute for verified rewards in reinforcement learning.

items.title: Researchers analyze unembedding matrix dynamics in language model pretraining, revealing early encoding of task information before readout expression in Pythia model [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers studied when language models acquire capabilities by examining the unembedding matrix, or readout, during pretraining. They found that models encode task information in hidden states before the readout expresses it, causing output-based timelines to conflate encoding and expression. Using a new method called parameter-trajectory crosscoding, they identified a narrow early window in Pythia's pretraining when the readout reorganizes and word categories become decodable, while hidden states already contain task information not yet reflected in outputs. To explore the effect of readout learning speed, the team pretrained small models with varying readout learning rates and observed that higher rates led to earlier readout development and closure of the gap between encoding and expression, without significantly affecting final loss. These findings suggest that early behavioral milestones in training may reflect when the readout learns to express information rather than when the model actually learns it.

items.title: Researchers introduce PremiseCheck, a framework combining LLM rewriting and decision models to efficiently fact-check peer review comments across NLP, machine learning, and natural sciences [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: PremiseCheck addresses the challenge of factual errors in peer review comments, which can misstate paper content and strain the review process amid growing submissions. The framework uses a large language model (LLM) to rewrite review comments into explicit premises without reading the entire paper, then applies a decision model to verify each premise against the paper. This approach achieves accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 at roughly half the cost and significantly reduced latency, particularly in NLP reviews. The researchers also introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels factual errors in review comments under a unified definition across multiple scientific fields, measuring accuracy alongside cost and latency. PremiseCheck improves over existing methods by efficiently handling comments that mix several implicit assertions, combining the strengths of expensive LLM checks and cheaper decision models to optimize fact-checking performance.

items.title: Researchers release ToolBottleneckBench to measure tool-agent performance under controlled pressures and fixed harness budgets across 21 configurations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: ToolBottleneckBench is a new benchmark designed to evaluate tool-agent performance by varying pressures such as the registered tool catalog, visible tool menu, certified workflow, and encoding of returned records while keeping synthetic enterprise tasks fixed. The benchmark uses an exact grader to identify the first unmet obligation in failed episodes and the harness limits that cause failures, revealing that the visible tool menu imposes the largest penalty on model performance, primarily due to truncation at the completion cap. Tests across 21 model and harness configurations show that increasing the completion cap significantly reduces penalties related to truncation. Most failures occur due to harness limits, and failure records do not reliably indicate the pressure causing the failure beyond tool call counts. The study also finds that certain repairs affecting tool access or call issuance outperform configuration changes, though none improve model behavior directly. The researchers recommend reporting pressure effects alongside the harness budgets used and have made the benchmark publicly available on GitHub.

items.title: Researchers find large language models share a working memory readout bottleneck due to interference rather than attention precision across multiple model families [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers analyzed 15 pretrained large language models (LLMs) from three families, ranging from 70 million to 14 billion parameters, and minimal transformers trained from scratch to investigate working memory limitations on the N-back task. They found that while attention mechanisms correctly locate target items, errors arise from interference caused by competing items during readout, rather than from imprecise attention focusing. Suppressing non-target item identities improved model sensitivity, especially in larger models where the task is distributed across more attention heads. The study distinguishes between two hypotheses for LLM working memory limits: a precision account where attention fails to focus on the correct item, and an interference account where correct items are attended but corrupted by competing content. Results showed that sharpening attention had minimal effect, whereas reducing interference significantly enhanced performance, aligning with interference-based theories of human working memory. In minimal transformers, a second attention layer helped overcome precision constraints, indicating that readout interference is the primary bottleneck in LLM working memory.

items.title: Researchers propose RaRE, a judge ensemble strategy for Rubrics as Rewards in reinforcement learning, improving performance by weighting confident judges and excluding high-disagreement cases [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: Researchers introduce RaRE (Rubrics as Rewards with Ensembles), a method that enhances reinforcement learning in non-verifiable domains by using multiple LLM judges to score responses against structured rubrics. RaRE employs a soft-Likert reward system that weights judges based on confidence and a drop-on-disagreement mask to exclude inconsistent evaluations, addressing score variability caused by judge identity. The study demonstrates that RaRE outperforms single-judge approaches on benchmarks like HealthBench and GPQA Diamond, leveraging the complementary strengths of different judges. This approach highlights judge ensembling as a promising direction for improving reinforcement learning with rubrics in complex evaluation settings.

items.title: Representation Redistribution in Sparse Autoencoders [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.21240v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose language model activations into sparse features, but prompt transformations designed to preserve the underlying request can redistribute activity across them. A feature change observed on one transformed prompt need not recur, and even a recurring change need not affect a downstream computation. We introduce the redistribution sensitivity score (RSS), which identifies large feature responses that recur in a consistent direction, and evaluate the resulting supports on variants excluded from selection. Across 27 pretrained SAEs spanning eight language models, the tested prompt transformations produce a reproducible redistribution profile on these excluded variants. We then separate recurring representation change from signed readout contribution and decision failure. For a fixed linear readout, an exact decomposition shows how response magnitude, readout coefficients, directional alignment, and the clean margin determine downstream consequences. In two frozen safety readouts, combining RSS support erosion with the full clean margin yields recurrent failure AUROCs of 0.935 and 0.958 using median supports of 20 and 19 features, compared with 0.965 and 0.964 using full erosion. RSS therefore provides a way to identify recurring sparse representation changes and quantify their contribution to a downstream readout without equating representation change with failure. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/Redistribution-Sensitivity-Score

items.title: System1-Arena: Which Decisions Can Be Left to System 1? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.21244v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) often make discrete decisions, such as flagging phishing or escalating to a human. System-1 models, such as Jev and the OpenAI Decisions API, return probabilities over options in a single forward pass, while System-2 approaches generate reasoning steps. Which decisions can System-1 models handle, and which require generative reasoning? We introduce System1-Arena, a benchmark that gives all models the same decision requests and scores their probabilities. It contains 92k questions across 105 tasks from 268 public sources, in four groups: text classification and knowledge, applied decisions, evaluation and control, and agent and action. It also includes 138 closed-loop environments, from web shopping and SWE-bench coding control to robotics, games, and driving; in real-time mode, the world evolves while a model decides. We evaluate 30 models: 7 closed LLMs, 13 open LLMs read at the answer token, and 10 System-1 models. The largest System-1 models match or exceed fast closed LLMs in non-agentic accuracy, with better-calibrated probabilities at one-quarter of the latency. A reasoning LLM is the most accurate, at about 70x the cost of a fast LLM. In closed loops, large open LLMs succeed most often (up to 32.9%); small System-1 models rarely succeed.

items.title: Behavioral Compositionality of Sparse Autoencoder Representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.21261v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) represent model activations with sparse, linearly decoded features, but the downstream effects of those features need not compose additively. We introduce SAE Additivity Residuals (SAR), which measure the behavioral variation left unexplained above a chosen interaction order. Under independent feature subset sampling, population SAR is exactly the normalized energy of interactions above that order and bounds coalition ordering error for the optimal low order approximation. To distinguish compositionality associated with the SAE representation from that induced by downstream computation, we compare learned SAE coordinates with sum preserving random rotations of the same selected subspace and find lower first order residuals for the learned coordinates across all 18 model and behavior settings. The coordinates are nevertheless not fully additive: pairwise terms improve held out coalition ordering in every setting and outperform parameter matched models using randomly selected third order terms. In a combined steering experiment, pairwise modeling raises rank fidelity from 0.5874 to 0.7790 and reduces ordering error from 0.1444 to 0.0606. Together, these results show that SAE coordinates support comparatively compositional behavioral descriptions while faithful joint explanations and interventions still require interactions beyond individual feature effects. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenSAE/SAE-Behavioral-Compositionality.

items.title: Trajectory-Level Speculation with Semantic Verification for Tool-Using Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.21463v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language model agents solve tasks through long sequences of tool calls, and the prevailing design has a single strong model generate every step, although many steps are routine enough for a much smaller model. Existing ways of sharing this work keep the strong model as the generator: routers and collaborative agents decide which model handles each query or step, and speculative methods check a small model's drafts one step at a time, usually against the strong model's own action. We introduce SpecAgent, a collaboration protocol that turns the strong model from the author of each step into a reviewer of steps drafted by a weak model. The weak model executes read-only tool calls as it drafts, so that every step is grounded in real observations, and holds the first action that would modify the environment. The strong model then verifies the drafted segment in a single prefill pass, commits the longest prefix it judges semantically valid, and repairs the first rejected step. Because verification replaces autoregressive decoding with parallel prefill, the strong model decodes only short verdicts and occasional repairs rather than every step. On $\tau^2$-Bench, SpecAgent comes within one point of the strong model's success rate while roughly halving memory traffic and wall time, and on AutomationBench and VitaBench it recovers 44-75% of the quality gap while lowering both. In an edge-cloud deployment on MCP-Atlas with three cloud models, it closes 53-75% of the weak-strong quality gap while the strong model generates at most half as many tokens. These results suggest that a strong model need not author every step of an agent: reviewing grounded drafts retains most of its quality while cutting both latency and memory traffic.

items.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.21561v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under the MIT license at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.

items.title: Human Interventions as Labels: Localizing, Steering, and (Sometimes) Editing the Computations Behind LLM Agent Failures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.21708v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When an LLM agent misbehaves, a human steps in, and that intervention is usually discarded or replayed as training data. We treat it instead as a measurement: a label pointing at the internal computation that failed. We study it in a controlled agent environment, on one failure (asking a clarifying question when the request was already unambiguous), with labels from a rule-based overseer validated against blind human judgment. Claims cover eligible models, which both over-ask and sometimes act on matched unambiguous requests: five of thirteen qualified (Qwen2.5-3B, gemma-2-2b, OLMo-3-7B, Mistral-Nemo-12B, Phi-4). Four findings. First, the ask-vs-act decision is causally localizable in every eligible family: a direction learned from intervention labels flips 72-100% of held-out over-asks at a definite residual-stream depth, with site and dose chosen on training data, and random directions under the same procedure flip at most one episode. Second, over-asking has two mechanistic signatures: in four families the model demonstrably knows the request is unambiguous (the belief is decodable, causally inert and orthogonal to the decision) and asks anyway; in the fifth, the rare over-asks track different world-representations. Third, steering gated on a probe readout removes most of the simulated oversight burden while legitimate questions survive (bootstrap 95% intervals exclude zero); a prompt instruction makes it worse. Fourth, consolidating the fix into the weights yields a map, not a rule: on one model a LoRA confined to the causal band passes every criterion fixed in advance while behavior cloning on identical data breaks retention; on three families the reverse holds; on the fifth the outcome crosses the boundary across seeds. A geometric rule written down in advance to predict the regime failed on two out-of-family tests; we report the failure and stop rather than fit a replacement.

items.title: FIRM: Fisher-Informed Retention Merging for Federated LLM Unlearning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.21720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Federated LLM unlearning addresses targeted knowledge removal when forget and retain data remain distributed across private clients and are inaccessible to the server. The resulting locally trained adapters encode conflicting objectives, making their aggregation fundamentally different from conventional federated optimization. A key failure mode is magnitude explosion, whereby unnormalized cross-client aggregation increases the merged update magnitude and degrades retained utility under stronger unlearning. We propose FIRM (Fisher-Informed Retention Merging), a single-round framework for stable and retention-aware server-side aggregation. FIRM uses client-local Fisher statistics as a unified sensitivity signal to construct a Fisher-normalized base merge and impose explicit control over retain-sensitive parameters. Its second-order retention projection admits a unique minimum-distance solution, while the corresponding dual scales with the number of retain clients rather than the model dimension. Experiments across WMDP, TOFU, and MUSE-HP using Zephyr-7B and Llama-3-8B show utility gains at comparable forgetting on WMDP and MUSE-HP, with metric-dependent trade-offs on TOFU. Controlled comparisons support benefits of the combined base merge and additional retention correction at selected operating points.

items.title: Reliable Knowledge Acquisition for Continual Learning Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.21739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As agents powered by foundation models move into open-ended environments, continual learning from experience becomes essential. For agents built on models with fixed parameters, this learning requires reusing prior task experience in context to improve performance and efficiency on future tasks. Existing memory and experience-learning systems typically focus on either retained facts or procedures, and lack a mechanism for establishing the reliability of claims extracted from the ongoing task stream. Indeed, we find that approximately 12--33\% of entries produced by representative systems harm future task performance when reused. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{RIKA} (Reliable Knowledge Acquisition), which combines hierarchical extraction of factual, conceptual, procedural, and metacognitive knowledge with Evidence-based Knowledge Admission, which uses source evidence and subsequent experience to govern which claims enter the task agent's context, without additional validation tasks. Across six task streams from Continual Learning Bench and four model backbones, RIKA achieves the highest aggregate score on every backbone.

items.title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22019v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier models, general-purpose and domain-specific alike, now include a midtraining stage between pretraining and post-training, but little has been published about how this stage is built. We present an open midtraining recipe that primes base models for agentic post-training, and we show its effectiveness on two Nemotron models of different sizes. Pretraining typically runs at short context and sees almost no agent interactions, while SFT data is mostly synthetic, and very long SFT stages can hurt the model's later RL trainability. Our midtraining stage sits between the two. It trains at 256K context for hundreds of billions of tokens on a diverse mixture of natural software-engineering data like packed repositories, pull requests, commit histories, and build logs together with a small share of agentic traces. On Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, 500B midtraining tokens improve SWE-bench Verified from 60.7 to 64.5, SWE-bench Multilingual from 55.8 to 62.8, and SWE-bench Pro from 32.0 to 35.5 after identical full SFT. On the larger Nemotron 3.5 Super, 280B midtraining tokens improve DeepSWE, a harder benchmark of long-horizon tasks, from 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified from 72.9 to 74.3 after identical full SFT. Midtraining also improves robustness across agent harnesses on both models. We report the ablations behind the recipe and an evaluation protocol built on short fixed SFT runs, since base-model proxy metrics did not correlate reliably with post-training results.

items.title: Selection Is Not Learning: Choosing Model Futures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22029v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving language models train on tasks they generate, so every round must decide which updated model the next round inherits. Current loops such as R-Zero, Agent0, and Skill Self-Play make this decision through the task, admitting tasks that look learnable and inheriting every resulting update. We identify a selection-to-update gap in these loops, where a task that looks learnable need not produce a useful update. Most updates on verified tasks fail to make correct answers more likely, yet these loops inherit them all. HeirCommit freezes the updated model and uses fresh evaluation questions to decide whether to inherit it or retain the current model. EvoHeir separates parameter inheritance from experience inheritance, using current and archived experience to repair failures and preserve successes before final confirmation. Our analysis characterizes selection-induced optimism and decomposes regret into selection, absorption, and confirmation errors. HeirCommit cuts the harmful share of accepted updates by 68-83% relative to random inheritance at the same acceptance rate. Across four backbones, EvoHeir achieves the best mathematics and general-reasoning averages, raising the math average by 5.3% relative to the strongest baseline, Agent0. The framework lets useful experience persist even when the model that produced it is not inherited.

items.title: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise in LLM Financial Forecasts [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22043v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Which inputs drive a language model's financial forecast? We construct synthetic earnings announcements that independently reverse 20-day momentum, non-informational commentary tone, and whether fixed actual EPS beats a manipulated consensus. Six instruction/chat checkpoint conversions from four families (0.49-7.61B base parameters) receive 2,016 prompts each under a direct-answer Q8_0 protocol. The design includes 24 numerical blocks, six commentary pairs, profits and losses, rising and falling annual EPS, and two surprise sizes. Both A/B answer assignments and U/D cover all 384 primary scenarios per conversion. We estimate matched changes in conditional answer-prefix scores, not calibrated market probabilities. Across these checkpoints, the primary EPS contrast ranges from -0.19 to 86.80 percentage points. The magnitude of the primary signed tone contrast exceeds that of EPS in 5 of six models, and momentum exceeds it in 5. Natural-word numerical diagnostic accuracy ranges from 51.0 to 95.8 percent. Answer-encoding, wording, context, and conversion controls qualify these results. The experiment measures observable input reliance and numerical recognition; it establishes neither an internal reasoning mechanism nor realized return predictability. Public benchmark prompts, recorded scores, and an interactive recorded-results explorer accompany the study.

items.title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22174v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session's advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.

items.title: Beyond Downstream QA: Rethinking How We Evaluate Agent Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22209v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent memory benchmarks evaluate whether an agent's responses reflect correct knowledge, measuring downstream question-answering accuracy as a proxy for memory quality. We show this evaluation paradigm is incomplete: it conflates memory correctness with retrieval and generation quality, producing both false positives where correct responses mask broken memory and false negatives where incorrect responses blame correct memory for retrieval failures. We introduce FEB-30, a benchmark of 30 fact-evolution trajectories spanning 6 diagnostic categories and 3 difficulty levels, constructed via paradigm inversion: documents are generated from known fact trajectories, yielding deterministic ground truth without human annotation. Each trajectory defines how a fact should evolve across multi-author artifacts (documents, emails, conversations), enabling direct inspection of the memory store after each ingestion step. Applying FEB-30 to a representative memory system, we demonstrate that intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation, and that failure modes differ systematically by category and difficulty. We release the benchmark, document generation pipeline, and scoring framework to support reproducible evaluation of agent memory systems.

items.title: Training-Free On-Policy Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22236v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation consolidates specialist models into one student at the price of rollouts, teacher passes and gradient steps for every teacher. We show that the consolidation does not need training: with forward passes only, the capabilities of separately tuned specialists can be aggregated into one model that is, on average, more accurate than either specialist alone. When specialists share a base model, distillation has an exact layer-wise solution: each linear layer of the fused model must reproduce every specialist's output on the inputs that specialist receives while reading its own answers, a least-squares problem whose solution needs only the second moments of those inputs. One forward pass over a few hundred rollouts provides them. We call this training-free on-policy distillation (\method). What the rollouts contain matters more than the solver: answers truncated in repetition loops are few among a mathematics specialist's rollouts but carry a large share of their tokens, and removing them lifts the fused model on AIME25 from task arithmetic's level to the specialist's at matched precision. On Olmo~3 7B, a few GPU-hours of forward computation per specialist yield a generalist that keeps most of each specialist's gain on each of seven mathematics and code benchmarks.

items.title: Language Is a Security Surface for Agent Guards [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22244v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Step-level guards decide, before each tool call, whether an agent's next action is safe given the user's request and the trajectory so far. Users write those requests in many languages, while guard prompts and the benchmarks on which purpose-built guards are trained and evaluated are English. We ask whether a guard's verdict depends on the language of the request. We build LinguaGuardBench from the 1,220 labelled steps of TS-Bench AgentDojo-Traj: we translate only the user instruction into German, French, Turkish, Swahili and Amharic, and keep every tool call, observation and label byte-identical, so any change in a verdict is attributable to language alone. Six English rewordings and a whitespace placebo serve as controls, and managed guards are run three times to measure their noise. Across 19 guards, from frontier APIs to 4B open models and four purpose-built agent guards, most open, small and purpose-built guards change verdicts under translation beyond their own noise floor, and the effect grows with the rarity of the language: among the nine guards below 13B parameters, the mean placebo-adjusted flip rate rises from +1.5 pp on French to +4.4 pp on Amharic. Purpose-built guards are the most sensitive. The direction of the damage tends to follow guard size: open guards of 12-30B parameters block more benign steps (up to +5.0 pp false positives), and every significant loss of recall is in a guard below 10B (up to -7.4 pp). Frontier guards shift by at most about one point; the strongest, Gemini 3.8 Flash, returns identical verdicts with and without the request. The damage is concentrated in a few instructions and, in a post-hoc analysis, falls on steps where the agent's reasoning restates the English request, consistent with guards reacting to inconsistency between channels. English paraphrase moves every guard less than translation does. We release the benchmark and all 489k verdicts.

items.title: Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22273v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.

items.title: Knowledge That Is Linear Before Fine-Tuning Generalizes After It [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Not all facts a language model can recall support further learning equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which can be recalled but do not support such generalization in a given task. We study this distinction by constructing new relations from existing ones. Take the relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris -> Europe) and assign each of its answers an arbitrary new label (Europe -> crab, Asia -> zebra). The new relation then maps Paris -> crab. We fine-tune the model on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the corresponding labels to held-out subjects that share an answer in the original relation. Having learned Paris -> crab, does it answer Munich -> crab? Across eleven language models and 70 relations, how linearly readable the original relation is in pretrained representations strongly predicts this generalization. Within each model, the two correlate across relations at Pearson r = 0.87 to 0.92. This association persists when controlling, separately and jointly, for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to re-randomizing the label assignment and fine-tuning seed, and to replacing the animal labels with labels from thirteen other semantic categories. When we map a fine-tuned model's wrong label back to the original answer it was assigned to, Munich -> zebra becomes Munich -> Asia. Answers recovered this way are more often among the linear probe's top answers for the subject than among the pretrained model's own. Whether a new relation generalizes depends less on whether its facts can be recalled than on how readily their shared structure can be read out linearly.

items.title: Twice Upon a Time: Complementary Representations for Time-Series Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.22327v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Time Series Language Models (TSLMs) enable language-based understanding and reasoning over temporal data, yet a fundamental question remains: what information should their time-series representations preserve, and what variation should they factor out? Existing TSLMs typically expose the language model to a single representation, imposing a fixed inductive bias across downstream tasks. We instead introduce complementary representations as a design principle for time-series reasoning. Our model combines two visual views: line plots preserve absolute measurements and the observed coordinate frame, while normalized delay embeddings factor out positive amplitude rescaling and offsets while exposing temporal structure. Dedicated visual encoders integrate both views into a shared language model through visual tokens and multi-level feature fusion. Evaluation-time interventions verify that the two views exhibit distinct invariance profiles, while single-view ablations show that their combination is particularly beneficial beyond basic perception, with the large gains in prediction and reasoning. Built on Qwen3-VL-8B, our dual-view model improves overall TSRBench accuracy from 44.5% with line plots alone to 53.2%, substantially exceeding the strongest evaluated dedicated TSLM baseline at 36.7%. It further achieves 89.9% accuracy on TSExam and 86.8% numerical accuracy on multivariate ChatTS alignment. Together, these results demonstrate that complementary representations provide an effective design principle for general-purpose TSLMs, enabling models to exploit temporal structure without sacrificing access to the original measurement frame.

items.title: ContinualSkillBench: Can LLM Agents Truly Evolve Their Capabilities? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.03874v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Modern agent frameworks equip large language models with external skill libraries to solve complex tasks. However, it remains unclear whether these systems can effectively evolve their skills and whether the resulting skills improve task-solving capabilities. To bridge this gap, we introduce ContinualSkillBench, a dynamic evaluation framework for in-context continual skill learning. It covers five domains, each with 100 tasks ordered by difficulty and opportunities for skill transfer. Our experiments show that sequential execution generally improves performance, but the gains vary substantially across models and domains. Moreover, across two models and three domains, retaining context and feedback without skill maintenance yields nearly the same mean performance as maintaining an explicit skill library. Explicit skills nevertheless provide selective benefits for tasks requiring reusable procedures or precise outputs. We further find that the weaker model (GPT-4o) accumulates more skills but reuses them less often, suggesting difficulty consolidating task-specific experience into reusable procedures. These findings show that current in-context skill evolution mechanisms can support continual adaptation, but still struggle to consistently consolidate experience into robust and transferable skills.

items.title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.14959v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

items.title: AI Scientists for Building Virtual-Cell Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2508.02276v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autonomous agents, from virtual laboratories to biological data-analysis agents and co-scientists, have begun to turn scientific goals into hypotheses. Whether they can go further and convert real, noisy and complex biological data into executable model hypotheses and architectures that encode testable assumptions remains unclear. Predicting how cells respond to genetic and chemical perturbations is a natural test of this ability: it is central to decoding disease mechanisms and therapeutic discovery, yet it demands cross-disciplinary expertise rarely concentrated in a single research group. Here, we introduce CellForge, an organized team of autonomous agents for single-cell perturbation modeling. Given a dataset and a task, it surveys the literature, parses the data, identifies relevant baselines, and formulates a model hypothesis through critic-mediated discussion among agents specialized in data modeling, single-cell biology, and deep learning. It then writes the training code, runs the experiments, and returns a trained predictor including architecture, code, and validation results. The architecture itself is the hypothesis: CellForge produces it end-to-end, with no human specifying the design, loss, or training protocol. Across six perturbation datasets spanning transcriptomic, epigenomic, and proteomic contexts, CellForge yields models that are competitive with hand-crafted state-of-the-art results on established tasks and extends the same workflow to paired multi-omic readouts. Blinded human evaluators rate CellForge's research plans as more scientifically sound and innovative than those from single LLMs or deep-research systems. In summary, we show autonomous agents can complete the full hypothesis-to-validation cycle in single-cell biology, with an AI effectively building another AI, in a complex setting that currently requires a team of human experts.

items.title: Learning Not To Interfere: Adapting Experts For Model Merging [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2603.13467v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Model merging has shown that multitask models can be created by directly combining the parameters of different models that are each specialized on tasks of interest. However, models trained independently on distinct tasks often exhibit interference that degrades the merged model's performance. To solve this problem, we formally define the notion of Cross-Task Interference as the drift in the representation of the merged model relative to its constituent models. Reducing cross-task interference is key to improving merging performance. To address this issue, we propose our method, Resolving Interference (RI), a light-weight adaptation framework which disentangles expert models to be functionally orthogonal to the space of other tasks, thereby reducing cross-task interference. RI does this whilst using only unlabeled auxiliary data as input (i.e., no task-data is needed), allowing it to be applied in data-scarce scenarios. RI consistently improves the performance of state-of-the-art merging methods by up to 3.8% and generalization to unseen domains by up to 2.3%. We also find RI to be robust to the source of auxiliary input while being significantly less sensitive to tuning of merging hyperparameters. Our codebase is available at: https://github.com/pramesh39/resolving_interference

items.title: LLMSurgeon: Diagnosing Data Mixture of Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2605.30348v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The pretraining data mixture of Large Language Models (LLMs) constitutes their "digital DNA", shaping model behaviors, capabilities, and failure modes. Yet this composition is rarely disclosed, making post-hoc auditing of data combination or provenance difficult. In this work, we formalize Data Mixture Surgery (DMS): given only generated text from a target LLM, estimate the domain-level distribution of its pretraining corpus under a predefined taxonomy. We propose $\textbf{{LLMSurgeon}}$, a strong framework that casts DMS as an inverse problem under the label-shift assumption. Rather than directly aggregating classifier outputs, LLMSurgeon estimates a calibrated $\textit{soft}$ confusion matrix and solves a constrained inverse problem to correct systematic domain confusion and recover the latent mixture prior. To evaluate, we introduce $\textbf{{LLMScan}}$, a recipe-verifiable evaluation suite built from open-source LLMs with transparent pretraining mixtures. Across LLMScan, LLMSurgeon recovers domain mixtures with high fidelity under fixed protocols. Our work presents a practical, post-hoc approach for auditing the digital DNA of foundation models without access to their training data.

items.title: Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing Training Influence to Learned Behavioral Policies [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2606.29171v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: While existing data attribution methods can identify which training examples build specific mechanistic circuits, they cannot explain how training data shapes the behavioral decisions a model learns. We introduce Symbolic Mechanistic Data Attribution (SMDA), a framework that attributes training pairs to the interpretable symbolic policies governing model behavior. SMDA fits a closed-form Ridge regression over sparse autoencoder (SAE) features to model a behavior, then decomposes how each supervised fine-tuning (SFT) example shifts that policy through feature-activation ($\Delta X$) and output-probability ($\Delta Y$) pathways. We distill a symbolic policy for refusal in Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct and analyze 200 SFT pairs. Our analysis reveals (1)~the symbolic policy's coefficients expose systematic gaps in the base model's safety behavior, such as religious stereotyping; (2)~per-feature $\Delta X/\Delta Y$ decomposition mechanistically explains why harmful and harmless pairs exert qualitatively different influences on certain features; and (3)~individual pairs routinely exhibit cross-feature interference, allowing SMDA to identify pairs whose dominant effect falls on unintended features. Retraining without such pairs improved accuracy by up to 4.5 percentage points over full fine-tuning. These results show that combining mechanistic interpretability with data attribution yields a diagnostic tool both more fine-grained than black-box influence functions and more scalable than manual circuit analysis.

items.title: Right Answer, Wrong Tokens: Tail-Aware Credit Calibration for RLVR [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.07976v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), GRPO-style methods can suffer from a positive-credit contamination failure mode. Specifically, uniform credit assignment can reinforce locally erroneous tail tokens alongside useful tokens within successful trajectories. To address this problem, we propose Tail-Aware Credit calibratiOn (TACO), which calibrates the positive credit assigned to such tokens without token-level error labels. To this end, TACO lets the policy serve as its own reference, assessing each sampled token's rarity relative to the policy's local expectations to compute a tail-risk score. Using this score as a proxy for potential local errors, TACO softly reduces positive credit for high tail-risk tokens while retaining nonzero weights, limiting their reinforcement without eliminating opportunities to learn useful rare patterns. Experiments across four LLMs and eight reasoning benchmarks show that TACO consistently improves over GRPO-style baselines. Notably, TACO also improves training stability, supporting sustained performance gains in long-horizon RL. The source code is available at: https://github.com/xiuyilou/TACO.

items.title: Amplitude-Only FFN Intervention for Tool-Structured LLM Inference: Method, Gated Evaluation Protocol, and Cross-Model Empirical Results [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2607.11183v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study Amplitude Gating (AG), an inference-time intervention that masks feed-forward network (FFN) activation coordinates while keeping pretrained weights fixed. Six SwiGLU sites separate shared and gate-only inputs, expanded gate/value channels, and the FFN output. Magnitude-ranked entropy masks and a Newton-Schulz windowed ranking variant provide alternative forward paths without retraining. The corrected September collection covers three Qwen checkpoints and eight text/tool endpoints. Under frozen local text scorers, the displayed Qwen3.5-9B non-NS configurations improve two function-call endpoints by +2.61 and +2.67 percentage points (pp), and static ToolBench in/out-domain endpoints by +1.64 and +2.82 pp. Comparing the lower historical/September AG mean with the higher baseline mean leaves positive margins on these routes. This supports robustness to the two observed executions, rather than formal statistical significance. JSON gains are small and displayed L-Eval effects are negative. These endpoints measure lexical or answer/action-name agreement rather than executed-tool success. Protocol-specific offline selector and Per-Sample Fix-Harm Evaluation (PFHE) analyses complement the fixed-route results. Current experimental data do not establish a significant random-forest (RF) benefit; further experiments are needed. AG provides a task-dependent intervention surface, with causal mechanisms, equal-budget advantages, repeated-run uncertainty, and serving cost still open.

items.title: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs? [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2608.25061v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GPUs increasingly accelerate database systems, but query-specific peak performance still often relies on hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks focus on machine learning operators, leaving irregular, heterogeneous, data-movement-heavy database-style operators untested. We introduce DataKernelBench, which translates SQL into validated PyTorch TorchPlan programs and evaluates LLMs that optimize either the core tensor-bounded snippet or the full query in CUDA or Triton through execution-guided repair. Across ten proprietary and open-weight models on TPC-H SF10 with an H100 GPU, the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves $2.11\times$ speedup over the TorchPlan baseline at full pass rate. We find that higher-performing implementations commonly use kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes, stronger models benefit most from full-query specialization, and workload context matters more than hardware context. To handle data larger than GPU memory, we extend TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading on TPC-H SF100 with four H100 GPUs, achieving $2.54\times$ speedup. Project page: https://kerneldf.github.io/datakernelbench

items.title: Language Models Can Control Their Own Attention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2609.02737v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models spend most of their attention on a small fraction of context, yet they read the entire KV cache to find the few tokens that matter. If the user asks about a previous detail in a 1M-token conversation, global attention layers must scan the full context to generate each token of the reply. A prominent approach pre-selects relevant tokens via lightweight proxy scores, but this extrinsic scoring still incurs O(N) per step. We take an intrinsic approach motivated by the simple question: wouldn't the model already know which parts of the context are relevant? We introduce Declarative Attention (DA), a protocol that elicits the model to declare where it needs to attend within its chain-of-thought, partitioning generation into three modes: (full context), (a specific region), and (recent output only). The inference engine parses these declarations like tool calls and skips most of the KV cache read. Under zero-shot evaluation across 15 long-context tasks, DA on off-the-shelf models (Gemma-4-31B, Qwen-3.6-27B) reduces total attended tokens per response (45.8%, 19.6%), despite extra decoding steps, with modest accuracy drops (1.40pp, 2.10pp) that shrink with model scale. DA unlocks a new axis of sparse attention, with further potential under training-based methods. Code is available at https://github.com/itsnamgyu/declarative-attention.

items.title: Minimal Witness Reinforcement Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.07226v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: ``What are the irreducible conditions that are sufficient to produce an outcome?'' is one of the most common questions that recur across computation and science. Its answers, the minimal sufficient witnesses, are what we mean by explanations, mechanisms and reasons. These problems usually ask for multiple minimal witnesses, yet standard RL methods may reveal only one solution or redundant ones. We formalize this problem as minimal-witness identification and introduce Minimal-Witness Reinforcement Learning (MWRL). MWRL takes the union of the sets certified by successful proposals sampled from the policy and credits each proposal for the coverage the group union would lose without that proposal. This credit assignment, derived directly from the problem definition, unifies the demands for minimality and recovery of alternatives from a single black-box verifier bit. Under this principle, we derive a value iteration planner that recovers the entire family of witnesses and a policy gradient method that can scale to large language models. Across different experimental settings, MWRL recovers most minimal witnesses, while other methods return redundant supersets or a single witness. By making witness families learnable from verifier feedback, MWRL expands the scope of reinforcement learning beyond single-solution optimization. Our code is available at https://github.com/TSUITUENYUE/MWRL.

items.title: Evaluating Model Capabilities After Benchmark Saturation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.20667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rapid advances in AI capabilities are causing benchmarks to saturate. Once several models approach perfect scores, a benchmark loses its power to differentiate between them, and with it its utility for informing AI safety cases and frontier policies. Yet benchmark items produce far more information than the scores we typically extract from them: a full transcript of how each model solved the task. We investigate whether these transcripts can be used to assess model capabilities even after benchmark scores have saturated. We simulate saturation retrospectively using historical benchmark and model releases, and test whether protocols that access only correctly solved transcripts from saturated benchmarks can predict capabilities measured on held-out, unsaturated items. We evaluate representative contemporary approaches for extracting information from model transcripts: pairwise judging, single-transcript absolute scoring, and predictions from deterministic transcript features or embeddings. We find that saturated transcripts retain capability information beyond benchmark accuracy. Amongst our evaluated protocols, pairwise judging performs best, reducing prediction error by 5.3 times compared to a baseline using only saturated benchmark scores. This capability-relevant information is distributed across transcript sections, but concentrated in specific channels of information such as reasoning and tool-calls. However, the predictive power of protocols does not always generalise across distribution shifts -- for example by underestimating the capabilities of the first reasoning models introduced in early 2025. Saturated benchmarks thus retain capability-predicting signal in their task transcripts, but extending the lifetime of existing benchmarks requires methods designed to extract these signals robustly.

items.title: Value-Informed Schedule Trimming for Accelerated Sequential Monte Carlo Guidance in Discrete Diffusion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.20669v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reward-guided discrete diffusion enables test-time alignment with downstream objectives, but applying Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) guidance at every denoising step is computationally expensive. Active guidance steps require additional reward evaluations and, for gradient-based proposals, value-gradient computations. Sparse guidance reduces this cost by guiding only a subset of timesteps, but commonly used schedules are fixed heuristics whose effectiveness can vary substantially across tasks. We propose VISTA, a training-free method that automatically selects guided timesteps under a fixed budget. VISTA formulates sparse guidance as approximation of the ideal full-guidance probability path and derives an estimable upper bound on \(\ell_1\) path deviation. Using value statistics collected from a small number of full-guidance warmup generations, VISTA optimizes the resulting empirical surrogate exactly via dynamic programming. The warmup generations can be retained as model outputs, and after schedule selection VISTA has the same per-generation guidance complexity as other sparse schedules with the same budget. Across text, biological sequence, and image generation tasks, VISTA discovers task-dependent schedules and outperforms hand-designed sparse schedules in most tested settings, while approaching or exceeding full-guidance performance on several task metrics. In toxic-text generation, for example, VISTA attains a 0.99 unique-toxic ratio compared with 1.00 for full guidance while reducing post-selection per-generation latency from 204.23 s to 38.16 s, a 5.35$\times$ speedup.

items.title: AlphaDiana: A Measurement System for Agents in Verifiable Reasoning Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.20675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agents pair reasoning models with harnesses that organize model calls, execute tools, load skill instructions, and retain history in memory. Understanding agent performance requires linking execution conditions to outcomes, behavior, and resource use. We introduce AlphaDiana, a measurement system with modular interfaces for datasets, agents, environments, and scorers. It preserves harness-native control loops while controlling file reuse and memory retention separately. AlphaDiana supports macro analyses of complete agents and micro interventions on agent components such as tools, skills, and memory under matched conditions. We study three open-source models and three open-source harnesses on five answer-based benchmarks, with two models also tested on two interactive benchmarks. We find that harnesses do not consistently improve the accuracy of reasoning: gains on questions unsolved by the model alone can be outweighed by losses on questions it answers correctly without tools. This inconsistency extends to component interventions: neither skill guidance nor retained history reliably improves accuracy. Behavior and output-token use must be assessed with correctness: low token entropy can accompany wrong answers, and less output per execution can mean more output tokens per correct answer when accuracy falls. AlphaDiana links answer correctness and execution status to traces and resource records for comparing agents and diagnosing failures under shared task and resource policies.

items.title: When Reality Outpaces Cognition: A New Scaling Principle for Reliable Intelligence [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.20764v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper challenges the understanding capabilities of existing AI paradigms and emerging world models by asking a fundamental question: How quickly can reality change before an intelligent system can no longer reliably perceive, reason, and act? We formulate this as a theory- and model-agnostic challenge in which systems must infer reliable actions for increasingly distant future states across a growing observation--reality gap. We operationalize this challenge through the effective Speed of Coherent Cognition (\(S_C^{\mathrm{eff}}\)), defined as the highest tested Speed of Reality (\(S_R\)) through which a system continuously satisfies a predefined behavioural reliability criterion from baseline. As a proof of concept, reinforcement-learning agents are trained at the baseline \(S_R\) and evaluated, without retraining, as \(S_R\) is increased by up to \(50\times\) while computational resources remain fixed. We compare Transformer and gated-MLP baselines with \(Co^4\), an architecture inspired by cellular mechanisms implicated in conscious processing and awake thought. Across the tested scenarios, \(Co^4\) achieves substantially higher \(S_C^{\mathrm{eff}}\) than the baselines, motivating \(S_C^{\mathrm{eff}}\) as a new benchmark and the scaling of coherent cognition as a principle for reliable AI.

items.title: ARIA: Runtime Inspection and Amendment for Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.20780v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS), a local mistake can propagate as other agents build on it, turning a correctable error into a failed task. Diagnosing completed runs or repeatedly re-executing them to search for corrections does not provide a learned policy for intervening while execution is still in progress. We present Agent Runtime Inspection and Amendment (ARIA), a framework for learning when and how to repair ongoing multi-agent executions. Our key intuition is to turn execution-verified repairs into reusable supervision, moving repair search into data construction and training so that a learned model can intervene at runtime without repeatedly testing alternatives. First, we collect over 24{,}000 successful and failed trajectories across four multi-agent frameworks, six benchmarks, and eight host models. From these trajectories, we construct the ARIA dataset, to our knowledge the first large-scale dataset pairing failed multi-agent trajectories with execution-verified repairs. It contains 3{,}953 verified repair pairs, each specifying what went wrong, where to intervene, and how execution should continue. Then, we develop the ARIA framework for MAS-agnostic runtime inspection and amendment, designed to integrate with any MAS that exposes execution trajectories and supports continuation replacement. Using verified repairs as training examples, we teach a compact model to recognize when intervention is needed and how to correct an ongoing run. The aim is to learn repair strategies that apply to related failures in new configurations, rather than merely reproduce individual corrections. Finally, the trained ARIA model demonstrates strong repair performance in both post-hoc and runtime settings, with generalization to unseen frameworks and host models. Our code is available at https://github.com/LabRAI/ARIA.

items.title: When Reasoning Traces Conflict with Evidence: How Answer Configuration Shapes Evidence Following [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.content_text: arXiv:2610.20805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A reasoning trace retained at answer time plays two roles: it can raise accuracy, and it can compete with the current evidence when the two disagree.
